item.title: 1763 Proclamation Line
item.snippet: This line was a legal division between British colonial settlement and Indigenous land. In 1763, King George III of Britain declared that British colonists should not settle in lands west of the Appalachian Mountains. The proclamation was supposed to end conflicts between colonists and indigenous groups on lands claimed by the British.
item.description:
This map shows a line drawn by British King George III in 1763 to mark a division between the British colonial settlement and land claimed by the British, but occupied by Indigenous Native American groups.

After the Seven Years War, which was called the French and Indian War in North America, the British claimed almost all of the land in North America East of the Mississippi River. This was part of the agreement in the 1763 Treaty of Paris with France and Spain.

The British claimed the land, but that did not mean they had control over the land. Many Indigenous groups lived on land claimed by Britain. Some of these groups had helped the British fight against France in the French and Indian War. Other Indigenous groups had been allied with France.

Many settlers in the British Colonies in the Eastern United States wanted to move West to the new lands claimed by Britain between the Appalachian Mountains and Mississippi River.

Many Indigenous groups in this area resisted the new British rule. Some had traded with the French and had fought against the British in the war. Others did not want new settlers from the British colonies settling their lands. Indigenous Native Americans, an Ottawa tribal chief named Pontiac, attacked British forts.

To try to end this conflict, the British King George III issued the Proclamation of 1763, closing land west of the Appalachian mountains to settlement. The proclamation did not end the conflict and angered colonial settlers.

Data: Historical Atlas of the United States. National Geographic Society, 1988.

item.title: Thirteen British Colonies
item.snippet: This National Geographic Society group layer shows the 1763 borders of the 13 British North American colonies that would become the United States.
item.description:
This map layer shows the 1763 borders of the 13 British North American colonies that would become the United States.

At the end of the Seven Years' War, which was called the French and Indian War in North America, the British claimed almost all of the land in North America East of the Mississippi River. This was part of the agreement in the 1763 Treaty of Paris with France and Spain.

The colonies were founded at different times during the 17th and 18th centuries. By 1763, each colony had slightly different government structures, but all were part of the British claims in North America and were ruled by the British government.

item.title: United States Battlefield Boundaries
item.snippet: This map layer shows the footprint of historic U.S. battlefields from the Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the War of 1812, and the Civil War (1861-1865) that are part of the National Park Service’s American Battlefield Protection Program.
item.description:
A battlefield is the current or historic location where an armed conflict or military battle takes place. You might be picturing an open field with soldiers based on the name. However, a battlefield is any place where a battle has taken place. For example, the Wilderness battle (May 5th to 7th, 1864) in the state of Virginia during the Civil War was fought in dense woodland. 

 

Many people consider battlefields to be sacred sites or hallowed ground. This is because of the number of people who died there in the conflict. Many people travel to these places to learn and honor the soldiers who sacrificed there.

 

This map layer shows the historic battlefields in the United States included in the National Park Service’s American Battlefield Protection Program. This program works to preserve and provide interpretation of these important places. By studying the past, we can learn from it and hopefully learn from the past mistakes of others. 

 

This map layer includes battlefields from 3 wars: the Revolutionary War (1775-1783), the War of 1812, and the Civil War (1861-1865). This layer includes two parts: one, the footprint of the entire battlefield, and two, the core area, where the fighting was the heaviest. The data for this map comes from two separate reports: the Report to Congress on the Historic Preservation of Revolutionary War and War of 1812 Sites in the United States (2007) and the Civil War Sites Advisory Commission Report on the Nation’s Civil War Battlefields (1993). 

 

Note: You are likely viewing this layer as part of a map on a specific war or battle. In that case, you may only see the battlefields for the specific event and not all three wars included in this dataset. This is not an error; the map maker has simply filtered the data to keep the map clear and concise.

item.title: Revolutionary War Battles
item.snippet: Explore the major battles of the Revolutionary War (1775 to 1783) with this map layer by the American Battlefield Trust, which works to preserve endangered battlefields across the United States.
item.description:
The United States Revolutionary War was a conflict between the Thirteen Colonies and Great Britain. The colonists, many of whom were British subjects, wanted more autonomy. The Colonies didn’t have any representatives in the British government. So, when Great Britain raised taxes on imported goods, like tea and molasses, many colonists believed this violated their rights as British citizens.  

In 1774, representatives from 12 of the 13 colonies met in Philadelphia at the First Continental Congress to organize their protests. By 1775, they were at war.  

The first battles, fought at Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts, were between American militiamen and British troops. Most of these militiamen weren’t professional soldiers, like the British troops. They were farmers, blacksmiths, and others from the community who volunteered to fight. Later that year, the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army, led by George Washington. 

In 1776, the Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence, and the American colonies became the United States of America. This allowed them to start making treaties with other European powers. The turning point in the war was the Battle of Saratoga, where an American force managed to capture a British army led by General Burgoyne. Following this defeat, France was convinced to send troops and ships to help the new nation, entering the war in 1778. 

By 1779, the war moved south. After several years of fighting from Virginia to Georgia, the Continental Army and French troops forced the surrender of British General Cornwallis’s army at Yorktown. This battle prompted the start of peace talks between Britain and the new nation of America. 

Information about the battles comes from two sources. The points showing when each battle occurred and who won it come from the American Battlefield Trust. The polygons showing where battles were fought comes from the National Park Service. Of these layers, the Core Areas polygons show where most of the fighting occurred. These areas are often described as hallowed ground. The Battlefield Boundary layer shows a larger area where areas of combat, command, communications, logistics, and medical services associated with the battle may be found. 

 

Data Citation: American Battlefield Trust. Maps. 2025 https://www.battlefields.org/search?algolia_search_index%5BrefinementList%5D%5Bfield_resource_type%5D%5B0%5D=map&ms=googlepaid&ms=googlepaid.

item.title: Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781
item.snippet: During the Revolutionary War (1775-1781), ports were key areas of military logistics, supplying food and supplies and moving troops. Explore a selection of key port cities along the east coast of North America, the Caribbean, and Great Britain from Jay Feyerabend’s master’s thesis, "Stonington’s Revolution: The role of small port towns in the American Revolution."
item.description:
What is a port?

A port is a place for ships to dock on the coast of an ocean, lake, sea, or river to unload or load cargo or passengers. These are essential places that play a key role in the transportation of goods and people. Ports are typically in places with enough land to build piers, wharves, warehouses, and loading and unloading facilities. Access to land transportation, such as roads and a large population center, is also key. Many ports also often have the capabilities for ships to be repaired. 

What is a Harbor?

Many ports are found on harbors, or protected bodies of water, where boats and ships often anchor. Harbors may occur naturally or be constructed by humans. An example of a naturally occurring harbor is Boston Harbor, part of Massachusetts Bay in the United States of America. The first human-engineered breakwater harbor in the United States was constructed near Lewes, Delaware, in 1828. It is not featured on this map. 

What is the role of a port during a war?

A key part of any military action is its ability to get supplies. This can include new equipment, medical supplies, food, and fresh troops. Ports are one way troops can be resupplied. There are already places where goods and people come through as part of a country's day-to-day economy. The side that controls the port has access to incoming supplies. During the Revolutionary War, the major port at New York City was divided. New York City had two governments: one under William Tryon, the royal governor, and a provincial congress of patriots seeking to separate from Great Britain. Merchants in the area were equally divided. Some felt that they needed Great Britain to access British markets, while others felt the British system limited their opportunities to make money. Over time, New York City and other large metropolitan areas, became more loyalist, while smaller ports tended to support the rebels. 

How was this map layer created?

The data for this map layer is from Jay Feyerabend’s master’s thesis, Stonington’s Revolution: The role of small port towns in the American Revolution. Their work explores the role key ports in early America played in the Revolutionary War. The map maker made a list of ports that appear in the thesis and categorized them as a major port, small port, Caribbean port, international port, Chesapeake port, river port/trade town, small port/inland port connection, and southern port. The ports were then separated into two groups: major port cities and ports that combined all other categories. 

Data Citation

Feyerabend, Jay. “Stonington's Revolution: The role of small port towns in the American Revolution” (2021), Master's Theses, 2020-Current. 74. https://commons.lib.jmu.edu/masters202029/74.
